newsitem.title: THAILAND: Pol Pot's ex-comrades say he is set to disappear.
newsitem.headline: Pol Pot's ex-comrades say he is set to disappear.

text.p: Former comrades of reviled Khmer Rouge strongman Pol Pot and senior Thai generals said on Tuesday that the chances of capturing the vanquished guerrilla leader were slim.
He was more likely to simply disappear from the public eye than be caught and tried for genocide during his 1975-79 Cambodian "killing fields" reign of terror, they told Reuters.
"I believe that he will slip away and mysteriously disappear," said a former senior official of the Khmer Rouge, who used to trek the jungles with Pol Pot in the early 1980s.
Pol Pot was last reported by Cambodian officials to be on the run in the country's northern mountain jungles after most of his remaining fighters had deserted him.

Cambodian First Prime Minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh said Pol Pot was heading towards the Thai border in a convoy of trucks after slaughtering his defence chief and 11 members of his family and abandoning his Anlong Veng stronghold.

"Rich men can do anything," said the source, who is now a senior member of the Khmer Rouge breakaway group called the Democratic National United Movement (DNUM) led by former Pol Pot ally and Khmer Rouge foreign minister Ieng Sary.
Pol Pot -- who has ample investments in Thailand -- was a millionaire with enough financial resources to arrange his departure and disappear from the scene, the source added.
Ieng Sary's break with the Khmer Rouge last August was the catalyst for thousands of defections. His troops have merged with the government, but the DNUM has remained an independent political arm.
Some Thai generals involved with the Cambodian conflict also said it was unlikely that Pol Pot would be arrested or killed.
"It is impossible to arrest or kill him, I believe that Pol Pot will mysteriously disappear or he may be reported killed but no one will see his body," said a general who declined to be identified.
It was quite likely that Pol Pot could slip into Thailand secretly and melt away into the populace, living incognito for the rest of his life, he said.
The general added that it was unlikely Pol Pot would flee to China, his close ally when he ruled Cambodia, because he had too many investments and monetary interests in Thailand through proxies.

The DNUM official said he was heartened to hear statements from Cambodian officials saying that another Khmer Rouge leader -- Khieu Samphan and the group's army commander, Ta Mok -- were willing to defect to the government.
"This is good news for the unity of the country," he said.
